clinicalPearls: Hyperekplexia, or startle disease, is defined by an exaggerated, non-habituating startle response to unexpected stimuli together with generalised stiffness.
Neonates present as stiff babies with marked hypertonia that characteristically disappears during sleep, alongside the exaggerated startle.
Tapping the tip of the nose or the glabella provokes a reproducible non-habituating startle, a useful bedside sign.
The major gene is GLRA1, encoding the glycine receptor alpha-1 subunit; GLRB, SLC6A5 (the glycine transporter GlyT2), GPHN and ARHGEF9 are also implicated.
Prolonged tonic stiffness in neonates can cause apnoea and sudden death, which is the principal life-threatening risk.
The Vigevano manoeuvre, forced flexion of the head and limbs towards the trunk, can abort a life-threatening tonic spasm and should be taught to carers.
Clonazepam, which enhances GABAergic inhibition, is the mainstay of treatment and is usually highly effective.
Consciousness is preserved during attacks and the interictal EEG is normal, distinguishing hyperekplexia from epileptic seizures.
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary hyperekplexia is a disorder of glycinergic neurotransmission, the principal inhibitory system of the brainstem and spinal cord. Most cases result from mutations in GLRA1, encoding the alpha-1 subunit of the postsynaptic glycine receptor, with further genes affecting the beta subunit (GLRB), the presynaptic glycine transporter GlyT2 (SLC6A5) and the postsynaptic clustering proteins gephyrin (GPHN) and collybistin (ARHGEF9). Impaired glycine receptor function or reduced glycine reuptake diminishes inhibitory postsynaptic currents onto motor neurons and interneurons, so a normally well-modulated startle circuit becomes disinhibited; minor unexpected auditory or tactile stimuli then evoke an exaggerated, non-habituating startle followed by sustained tonic muscle contraction. In neonates this disinhibition can produce dangerous generalised stiffness with impaired ventilation and apnoea. Inheritance is most often autosomal dominant through GLRA1, but autosomal recessive and other patterns occur, and an acquired antibody-mediated form should be considered when onset is in later life.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal or epileptic seizures, including startle-provoked epilepsy
Neonatal tetanus with trismus, risus sardonicus and a relevant cord-infection history
Stiff person syndrome and the related PERM (progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus) in older patients
Symptomatic hyperekplexia from a structural brainstem lesion
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of a panel including GLRA1, GLRB, SLC6A5, GPHN and ARHGEF9
Clinical elicitation of the non-habituating startle using the nose-tap or glabellar tap sign
EEG, which is typically normal during attacks and helps distinguish the disorder from epilepsy, ideally with video-EEG capture of an event
MRI of the brain, usually normal, to exclude a structural or brainstem lesion
Metabolic and septic screen in a stiff neonate to exclude mimics such as tetanus and sepsis
Anti-glycine receptor and anti-GAD antibodies where an acquired or adult-onset form is suspected
redFlags: Apnoea, cyanosis or bradycardia during prolonged tonic stiffness in a neonate, indicating the risk of sudden death
Recurrent unexplained falls with injury, falling stiffly like a statue without protective reflexes
Feeding difficulty or aspiration resulting from sustained stiffness
Progressive course with brainstem signs or autonomic instability suggesting acquired PERM rather than the hereditary form
reference.prognosis: Neonatal stiffness and the associated apnoea risk usually improve markedly over the first years of life and respond well to clonazepam. Most affected children have normal cognition and a good long-term outlook, although an excessive startle response and occasional falls may persist into adulthood.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the disorder as epilepsy and starting inappropriate antiepileptic drugs.
Failing to teach carers the Vigevano flexion manoeuvre to abort life-threatening spasms.
Overlooking the risk of apnoea and sudden death in affected neonates.
Confusing the stiff neonate with neonatal tetanus or sepsis.
Not distinguishing hereditary hyperekplexia from an acquired antibody-mediated form when onset is later in life.
references: Principles and practice of medical genetics
